subject: Agriculture
title: Agrivoltaics
description: A quick, practical guide to Agrivoltaics.

hook.text: Solar panels above, crops below—agrivoltaics grows food and generates electricity on the same land.

buildup.text: Traditional solar farms compete with agriculture for land. Agrivoltaics eliminates the conflict entirely.

discovery.text: Crops under solar panels receive partial shade that reduces water needs by 15–30% in hot climates.

twist.text: Some crops—lettuce, peppers, tomatoes—actually yield more under solar panels because excess heat harms them.

climax.text: Japan leads agrivoltaics with over 2,000 installations. Farmers earn dual income—from crops and electricity.

punchline.text: Same land, two harvests—food and energy. The sun gives enough for both.

quiz.question: Why do some crops yield more under solar panels?
options: Partial shade reduces heat stress and water loss in hot climates

details.summary: Agrivoltaics combines solar energy generation with crop or livestock production on the same land. This topic covers dual-use designs, shade-tolerant crops, and how agrivoltaic systems can boost farm income while generating clean energy.
details.whyItMatters: Land competition between food and energy production is intensifying. Agrivoltaics solves this by letting the same acre produce both crops and electricity, increasing total land productivity by 60–70%.
takeaways: Solar panels can shade crops that benefit from reduced heat stress in hot climates
Farmers earn revenue from electricity sales alongside their crop income
Agrivoltaic systems reduce soil evaporation, lowering irrigation needs

faq.question: What is agrivoltaics and how does it work?
faq.answer: Agrivoltaics installs elevated or spaced solar panels above cropland so that both farming and electricity generation occur on the same land. Panels are positioned to allow sufficient light for crops while producing renewable energy overhead.

faq.question: Which crops grow well under solar panels?
faq.answer: Shade-tolerant crops like lettuce, spinach, kale, potatoes, and certain berries perform well or even better under partial shade from solar panels, especially in hot climates where reduced heat stress and evaporation benefit plant growth.
